title: Rhodes, Milner and the Round Table network

countries.note: Rhodes's trustees, Milner, the Round Table journal (from 1910), Chatham House (1920) and the Pilgrims Society's London branch. Members held the posts of War Cabinet minister (Milner, 1916–18), the prime minister's private secretary (Philip Kerr, 1916–21) and editor of The Times (Geoffrey Dawson, 1912–19 and 1923–41).

Milner was High Commissioner from 1897. After 1902 his young staff ran the Transvaal and Orange River Colony administrations and worked for the 1910 Union. Patrick Duncan, one of them, became Governor-General in 1937.
Round Table group from 1909; Earl Grey, a Rhodes trustee, was Governor General 1904–11.
Round Table group from 1910; Quigley names Australia and Canada as the first dominion institutes of international affairs (1927).
Round Table group from 1910.

The Council on Foreign Relations, founded in 1921 after the 1919 Hotel Majestic agreement in Paris, and the Pilgrims Society's New York branch (1903). The CFR's War and Peace Studies project sent memoranda to the State Department from 1939 to 1945.

summary: Cecil Rhodes's wills from 1877 onward left his fortune to found a society to extend British rule. Carroll Quigley, a Georgetown historian who read the group's papers, dates its founding to a meeting of Rhodes, the journalist W. T. Stead and Reginald Brett (later Lord Esher) in February 1891. After the Boer War, Alfred Milner, High Commissioner in South Africa, brought young Oxford graduates into the colonial administration — his 'Kindergarten' — and they worked toward the Union of South Africa in 1910. The same men founded the Round Table in 1909–10, with a quarterly journal and groups in Canada, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa. During and after the First World War, members held posts close to the British prime minister and the press. At the 1919 Paris peace conference British and American delegates agreed to found institutes of international affairs; Chatham House followed in 1920 and the Council on Foreign Relations in 1921. Quigley traced this group through the 1940s; the CFR's own history records its wartime planning for the State Department.
uncertain: That these bodies formed one continuous society with an inner circle is Quigley's reading of papers he was shown; the bodies themselves were public and the offices their members held are on the record. His statement that the CFR was a front for J. P. Morgan & Co. rests on him alone. Quigley himself wrote that he approved of the group's aims and objected only to its secrecy.

confirmed_by.title: Carroll Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment (written 1949, published 1981)
Carroll Quigley, Tragedy and Hope (1966)
Council on Foreign Relations, centennial history (2021)

implications: Nearly everyone in this pattern held office openly and was appointed through normal channels. What it shows is how few doors those channels had. For about half a century, a few hundred people from the same Oxford colleges, the same South African administration and the same London dining clubs supplied the private secretaries, editors, governors and planners who shaped British and then American foreign policy. Voters chose the party; the papers its ministers read on the empire, Germany or the post-war order were often drafted inside this circle. The practical lesson is to look past who wins an election to who staffs the offices and writes the briefings.

title: The anticommunist web, 1945–1990

countries.note: Gladio, disclosed by Prime Minister Andreotti on 24 October 1990, and P2, whose 1981 list held the heads of all three intelligence services. Italy is where the stay-behind and lodge networks overlapped most.
The Chilean intelligence service DINA under Manuel Contreras called the founding meeting of Operation Condor in Santiago in November 1975.
CIA support for the stay-behind networks is confirmed in the Italian and Belgian inquiries; Condor's 1976 bombing of Orlando Letelier in Washington was carried out by DINA agents.

summary: From the late 1940s NATO's Clandestine Planning Committee, and from 1958 the Allied Clandestine Committee, coordinated secret 'stay-behind' networks with hidden arms caches in member and neutral countries. Italy's, called Gladio, was disclosed by Prime Minister Giulio Andreotti in October 1990; parliaments in Belgium and Switzerland opened inquiries the same year. Alongside them grew cross-border bodies run by the same milieu of officers and intelligence men: Licio Gelli's P2 lodge in Italy and Argentina, Aginter Press in Lisbon, the World Anti-Communist League from 1966, Operation Condor among six South American intelligence services from 1975, and the Safari Club joining the intelligence chiefs of France, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Iran and Morocco from 1976. Most were exposed only after a government changed, a parliament ordered an inquiry, or files were found — Paraguay's 'Archives of Terror' in 1992.
uncertain: No court has found that the stay-behind networks as such carried out the bombings of Italy's 'years of lead'; courts convicted individual neo-fascists and officers who obstructed the investigations, including P2 members. A single directing centre for all these bodies is not documented. What is documented is overlapping membership, shared training and money.

confirmed_by.title: European Parliament resolution on Gladio, 22 November 1990
Belgian Senate parliamentary inquiry on stay-behind networks, 1991
US National Security Archive, Operation Condor briefing books

implications: These networks were built to resist a Soviet invasion that never came. With no invasion, their people, weapons and secrecy were turned on domestic opponents: Condor killed exiles in Buenos Aires and Washington and shot one in Rome; P2 members sat at the head of Italy's intelligence services during a decade of bombings and steered the inquiries into them. Voters in most of these countries learned the networks existed only in 1990 or later. For a reader, the pattern is that secret structures set up for an emergency rarely close when the emergency passes, and the bodies meant to oversee them are usually the last to find out.

title: Banks that carried the hidden money
roles: Where officials were paid or deposits lost

countries.note: The Institute for the Works of Religion (IOR), whose letters of comfort stood behind Banco Ambrosiano's lending to Panama-registered shell companies. It paid creditors $224 million in 1984, citing 'moral involvement'.
Banco Ambrosiano (Milan), chaired by P2 member Roberto Calvi until his death in London in June 1982; and Michele Sindona's Banca Privata Italiana, which failed in 1974.
BCCI Holdings was registered in Luxembourg, with its operating centre in London; regulators in several countries closed it on 5 July 1991.
The ruler of Abu Dhabi and his government held about 77% of BCCI when it was closed (US Senate Kerry–Brown report, 1992).
Nugan Hand Bank, Sydney, collapsed in 1980 after co-founder Frank Nugan was found shot dead; its staff included retired senior US military and intelligence officers.
Banco Ambrosiano Overseas in Nassau, with Archbishop Paul Marcinkus of the IOR on its board.
Banco Ambrosiano Andino in Lima held much of the lending that disappeared; BCCI also held Peru's central bank reserves.
Ambrosiano's bank in Managua, whose licence the government cancelled in 1985.
BCCI's operating headquarters at Leadenhall Street; Calvi was found hanging under Blackfriars Bridge.

countries.role: Where officials were paid or deposits lost
countries.note: BCCI secretly owned First American Bankshares in Washington through nominees; former Defense Secretary Clark Clifford, its chairman, was indicted in 1992 (charges dropped for ill health). The CIA held accounts at BCCI.

summary: Four banks on this map grew because powerful customers needed money moved without questions. Banco Ambrosiano, chaired by P2 member Roberto Calvi, lent about $1.3 billion to shell companies in Panama and elsewhere backed by letters from the Vatican Bank, and collapsed in 1982. Michele Sindona, another P2 member, ran banks in Italy and New York that failed in 1974; he was later convicted of ordering the murder of the lawyer liquidating them. BCCI, founded in 1972 by Agha Hasan Abedi with Gulf money, secretly bought a Washington bank holding company, kept accounts for Manuel Noriega and for the CIA, paid officials of central banks in Latin America, and was closed by regulators in seven countries in July 1991. Nugan Hand in Sydney, whose staff included retired US generals and admirals and whose lawyer was former CIA director William Colby, collapsed in 1980.
uncertain: Australia's Stewart Royal Commission (1985) found no proof that Nugan Hand was a CIA operation. The Vatican paid Ambrosiano's creditors without admitting legal liability. No one has been convicted of Calvi's murder; five people were acquitted in 2007.

confirmed_by.title: US Senate, The BCCI Affair (Kerry–Brown report), 1992
Bank of Italy inquiry into Banco Ambrosiano, 1981–82
Royal Commission of Inquiry into Drug Trafficking (Stewart), 1983–85

implications: Each of these banks was licensed and supervised, and regulators saw warnings years before each collapse. They kept going because their customers included a church, intelligence services, a dictator and an oil state — institutions that publicly oppose crime but also need secret money channels. When the banks failed, depositors and small creditors took the losses and the officials who had used them were rarely charged. For a reader, the lesson is that banking secrecy is not only a tool of criminals; governments and institutions rely on it too, which is why they are slow to close the banks that serve them.

title: Lodges inside police forces and courts
summary: In police forces and courts, lodge membership matters because officers and judges are supposed to owe loyalty only to the law. Stephen Knight's The Brotherhood (1983–84) described Masonic lodges inside London's Metropolitan Police; the House of Commons Home Affairs Committee reported on Freemasonry in the police and judiciary in 1997 and 1999, and from 1998 new judges and police officers in England and Wales had to declare membership, a rule repealed for judges in 2009 and restored for the Metropolitan Police in 2025. In Italy the P2 list of 1981 held the Carabinieri and Guardia di Finanza commanders and 195 officers, and the parliamentary Anti-Mafia Commission seized lodge membership lists in 2017 after finding 193 lodge members in mafia proceedings. In the United States the Klan of the 1920s enrolled police chiefs and judges in Denver, Indiana and Alabama.
uncertain: How far lodge ties changed specific promotions or verdicts is rarely proven case by case; the UK committees found the belief that it did was widespread and damaging, but did not find a systematic conspiracy.

confirmed_by.title: House of Commons Home Affairs Committee, Freemasonry in the Police and the Judiciary, 1997; Freemasonry in Public Life, 1999
Italian Parliamentary Anti-Mafia Commission, report on Freemasonry, December 2017

implications: A person arrested or taken to court cannot see whether the officer, prosecutor or judge shares a private oath with the other side. That is why, even where no case was fixed, governments in Britain and Italy decided the public had a right to know who belonged. The record here shows both problems: lists that took parliaments years to obtain, and individual cases — a false arrest settled for £170,000, a Calabrian lawyer convicted with the 'Ndrangheta — where a lodge connection was part of the story. The general lesson is that justice depends on loyalties being visible, and secret ones undermine trust even when they do not change outcomes.

title: Sworn brotherhoods that chose who governed

countries.note: Every prime minister and state president from D. F. Malan (1948) to F. W. de Klerk (1989–94) was a member of the Afrikaner Broederbond, a secret Afrikaner men's society founded in 1918. Its membership list was published by journalists Ivor Wilkins and Hans Strydom in 1978.

Army officers who later founded the Black Hand killed King Alexander Obrenović in 1903 and its leader, Colonel Dragutin Dimitrijević 'Apis', became head of military intelligence; its rival, the White Hand, put General Petar Živković in power as prime minister in 1929.
IDEA, a secret society of army officers, prepared the April 1967 coup; the colonels ruled until 1974 and were tried in 1975.

The Society of St. Tammany ran New York City's Democratic machine; the Know Nothings won Massachusetts in 1854; the 1920s Klan elected governors in Indiana, Colorado and Oregon and helped send Hugo Black to the Senate and then the Supreme Court.

summary: In some countries a sworn society did not infiltrate the government — it decided who formed one. South Africa's Broederbond, founded in 1918, counted every apartheid-era prime minister and state president among its members and placed members across the civil service, universities and the broadcasting authority. In Serbia army officers who went on to form the Black Hand murdered the king in 1903, and its leader later ran military intelligence; in Greece a secret officers' society, IDEA, prepared the 1967 coup. In North America lodges and sworn orders built political machines: Tammany in New York, the Know Nothings in the 1850s, the Orange Order in Toronto city hall, the Ordre de Jacques-Cartier in French Canada, and the Ku Klux Klan of the 1920s, which elected governors and a future Supreme Court justice.
uncertain: Membership of a society is documented for each officeholder here; how much of each government's policy was decided inside the society rather than in cabinet is a matter of historians' judgement, strongest for the Broederbond, whose own documents set out its aims.

confirmed_by.title: Ivor Wilkins and Hans Strydom, The Super-Afrikaners (1978)
Greek junta trials, 1975
Indiana and Colorado Klan histories; Hugo Black's radio address, 1 October 1937

implications: Where one society chooses the leaders, an election only decides which of its members holds the job. South Africans who were not white Afrikaner men had no route into the Broederbond, so they had no route into the circle that picked their rulers for 46 years. The same mechanism appears in the other cases at smaller scale: a city run by a lodge, a state run by the Klan, an army run by a secret officers' society. For a reader, the pattern is that the most complete capture does not look like infiltration at all — it looks like ordinary government, because the society's members are the government.

title: Faith movements placing members in the state
summary: Several religious movements treat placing members in public office as part of their mission. Opus Dei members ran Spain's economic ministries from 1957 and held eleven seats in Franco's 1969 cabinet. The Gülen movement spent decades placing graduates of its schools in Turkey's police and courts; after the 2016 coup attempt the state dismissed more than 150,000 people as members. The Unification Church built ties to Japan's ruling party from its founder's alliance with former prime minister Nobusuke Kishi; the party's own 2022 survey found 179 of its 379 lawmakers had dealings with it, and a Tokyo court ordered the church dissolved in 2025. In South Korea, Shincheonji's leader was indicted in 2026 over 56,472 followers signed up to the ruling party. Scientology's Operation Snow White placed agents inside the US tax service and Justice Department in the 1970s; eleven members were convicted.
uncertain: Several of these placements rest on membership alone. Membership of Opus Dei or the RSS is not secret and is not misconduct; the cases count only where a forum or the organisation's own record ties the membership to an office. The scale of the Gülen network inside the Turkish state is documented mainly by Turkish government proceedings that critics say were also used against non-members.

confirmed_by.title: LDP internal survey on Unification Church ties, 8 September 2022
Tokyo District Court dissolution order, 25 March 2025
US v. Mary Sue Hubbard et al., D.D.C., 1979
Turkish government decrees under the 2016 state of emergency

implications: A movement that tells its members to seek public office is not breaking any law; many democracies welcome religious citizens in government. The problem appears when the movement's own hierarchy, not the voters or the civil service, decides who rises and what they do there — when a minister's first loyalty is to an organisation the public cannot see into. The Turkish case shows the other side: once a government decides a movement has infiltrated it, it can dismiss tens of thousands on evidence such as a banking app or a newspaper subscription. For a reader, the pattern is that hidden placement and mass purges are two ends of the same problem: nobody outside knew who belonged.

title: Movements that sought the state itself

countries.note: A military court convicted Brigadier Ali Khan and four majors in 2012 of links to Hizb ut-Tahrir.
The army said in January 2012 it had stopped a coup by serving and retired officers linked to Hizb ut-Tahrir.

summary: Two transnational Islamist movements on this map aimed not at placing members inside governments but at taking them over. The Muslim Brotherhood, founded in Egypt in 1928, won Egypt's presidency through Mohamed Morsi in 2012, led Tunisia's government through Ennahda from 2011 to 2014, held parliamentary seats and cabinet posts in Kuwait and Jordan, and, through Sudan's National Islamic Front, joined the 1989 coup that brought Omar al-Bashir to power. Egypt designated it a terrorist organisation in December 2013, Saudi Arabia and the UAE in 2014, and Jordan banned it in April 2025 while its party held 31 seats. Hizb ut-Tahrir, founded in Jerusalem in 1953, works openly for a caliphate and has repeatedly tried to recruit army officers; Pakistan and Bangladesh exposed cells in their armies in 2011–12, and Indonesia banned it in 2017.
uncertain: Governments that ban these movements also use the bans against peaceful opponents, and some designations followed elections the movements won. Whether a given officeholder acted on the movement's instructions is rarely established in court.

confirmed_by.title: Egyptian cabinet designation, 25 December 2013
Pakistan Army field general court martial, August 2012

implications: These movements show the line between infiltration and politics is not fixed. When the Brotherhood won elections it took office openly; its opponents then described its officials as infiltrators and removed them, in Egypt by a military coup. Hizb ut-Tahrir's approach of recruiting officers is closer to infiltration in the plain sense, and every country where it was found responded with arrests. For a reader, the pattern is that 'infiltration' is also a label governments use, and the facts underneath — elected office, army cells, mass bans — need to be read case by case.

title: French lodges and African presidencies
roles: Head of state or minister in a lodge
case_role: Head of state or minister in a lodge

countries.note: The Grande Loge Nationale Française and the Grand Orient de France sponsored or chartered lodges in former colonies; the GLNF's grand master installed Ali Bongo as grand master of Gabon's lodge in 2009. Jacques Foccart's Service d'Action Civique ran France's African networks from the Élysée.

summary: In former French colonies, Masonic lodges linked to Paris became a meeting place for presidents, ministers and French officials. Omar Bongo of Gabon was grand master of the Grande Loge du Gabon; his son Ali Bongo was installed as grand master in 2009 by the head of the Grande Loge Nationale Française. Denis Sassou-Nguesso of Congo, Idriss Déby of Chad, Mamadou Tandja of Niger and François Bozizé of the Central African Republic have been reported as lodge members, as have, in Jeune Afrique's 2012 survey, Blaise Compaoré, Amadou Toumani Touré, Alpha Condé and Abdoulaye Wade. Cameroon's president Paul Biya paid large sums to a French esoteric Templar order in the 1990s, as Le Monde reported in 1999.
uncertain: Most memberships here are reported by journalists rather than confirmed by the lodges, which do not publish lists. Whether lodge ties decided French policy toward these governments is not documented.

confirmed_by.title: Jeune Afrique, investigation of Freemasonry in Africa, 2012
Le Monde, 1999, on payments to the Ordre Souverain du Temple Initiatique

implications: Several of these presidents ruled for decades with French military and financial backing, and the lodges were one of the private spaces where that relationship was kept up — out of sight of parliaments in Paris and of citizens in Libreville or Brazzaville. A citizen of Gabon could not know that the head of state and the police chief were grand masters of lodges sponsored from France. For a reader, the pattern shows how a former colonial power's influence can continue through private networks after the flag is lowered.

title: One state's networks inside another

countries.note: The Chinese Communist Party's United Front Work Department directs 'united front' work among overseas Chinese and foreign elites.

In the 1970s the Korean Central Intelligence Agency and businessman Tongsun Park paid US congressmen ('Koreagate'); the House Fraser subcommittee (1978) also examined the KCIA's use of Sun Myung Moon's organisations.
The Russkiy Mir Foundation (2007) and the Voice of Europe network, sanctioned by the Czech government in March 2024 for paying European politicians.

summary: Some organisations on this map are run by one government to recruit officials of another. China's United Front Work Department appears in cases in Australia (Senator Sam Dastyari resigned in 2017; Di Sanh Duong was convicted of foreign interference in 2023), the United Kingdom (an MI5 alert on Christine Lee, 2022), Canada (the public inquiry into foreign interference, 2024–25), the United States (Linda Sun, an aide to New York's governor, indicted in 2024) and Taiwan, where courts convicted party leaders and candidates funded through Chinese 'united front' bodies. In the 1970s South Korea's intelligence agency paid US congressmen through Tongsun Park; in 2024 the Czech government sanctioned the Voice of Europe network for paying European politicians on Russia's behalf.
uncertain: Several cases named here ended without conviction, and forums in Canada and the UK found some suspicions well-grounded but unproven. Not every contact with a Chinese or Russian organisation is interference; the cases are here because a forum examined them.

confirmed_by.title: Public Inquiry into Foreign Interference in Federal Electoral Processes and Democratic Institutions (Hogue), Canada, 2025
MI5 interference alert, January 2022; Investigatory Powers Tribunal, 2024
US House Subcommittee on International Organizations (Fraser), report, October 1978

implications: These networks work through ordinary-looking channels: donations, community associations, trips, business partners and help at election time. The official who accepts them may not know who is behind them, and voters usually cannot tell. That is why Australia (2018), the UK (2023) and Canada (2024) passed laws requiring people acting for foreign states to register. For a reader, the pattern is that influence over a government can now be bought from abroad through the same routes domestic lobbyists use, and only disclosure rules make it visible.

title: Private forums where officials meet money
summary: A set of invitation-only bodies brings sitting officials together with bankers, executives and editors, usually without public minutes. The Bilderberg Meetings began in 1954; the Trilateral Commission was founded by David Rockefeller in 1973, and when its member Jimmy Carter became US president in 1977 he appointed fellow members as vice-president, secretary of state, defence secretary, treasury secretary and national security adviser. The Council on Foreign Relations' members filled much of the US foreign-policy establishment after 1945. Yale's Skull and Bones produced a CIA director and both 2004 presidential nominees. ALEC, founded in 1973, gives state legislators model bills drafted with corporate members; Florida's 2005 'stand your ground' law became an ALEC model. The World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders programme counts several heads of government among its alumni.
uncertain: Membership of these forums is mostly public and legal. That a forum decided a policy, rather than its members deciding it in office, is rarely documented; the cases here are placements and model bills, not secret decisions.

confirmed_by.title: Christian Science Monitor, 1980, on Trilateral Commission members in the Carter administration
ALEC Exposed (Center for Media and Democracy), 2011

implications: Nothing here is hidden in the way a lodge list is hidden; the names are often printed. What is hidden is the conversation: officials who will later regulate banks or negotiate treaties spend days with the people affected, off the record, and the same people meet again in the next administration. Ordinary citizens and smaller businesses have no seat at these tables. For a reader, the pattern is that access, not secrecy, is the advantage — and that a government can be shaped without anyone breaking a rule.

title: Exposure, purge and reversal

timeline.event: US Senate Church Committee begins hearings on intelligence abuses
Italian police find the P2 list at Licio Gelli's villa (17 March)
Andreotti discloses Gladio to the Italian parliament (24 October)
Regulators in seven countries close BCCI (5 July)
Paraguay's 'Archives of Terror' found in Lambaré (22 December)
Turkey begins mass dismissals after the 15 July coup attempt
Australia passes its foreign interference and foreign influence transparency laws
Tokyo District Court orders the Unification Church dissolved (25 March)

summary: Across countries and decades the record moves in the same three steps. A raid, a defector, a change of government or a parliamentary inquiry exposes a network: the P2 list in 1981, Gladio in 1990, the Broederbond membership in 1978, BCCI in 1991, the Unification Church's ties to Japan's ruling party after 2022. A government then bans the organisation or purges its members, sometimes with a law written for the purpose — Italy's 1982 law dissolving P2, Turkey's post-2016 decrees, Egypt's 2013 terrorist designation of the Brotherhood. Years later courts often narrow or reverse the findings: the P2 conspiracy charges ended in acquittals in 1994–96, Turkey's Ergenekon and Sledgehammer convictions were annulled in 2015–16, and Cardinal Becciu's Vatican conviction was set aside in 2026.
uncertain: The three steps are a pattern in this map's records, not a law; many exposures led to no purge, and many purges were never reviewed.

confirmed_by.title: Italian Law no. 17 of 25 January 1982
Turkish Constitutional Court and Court of Cassation rulings on Ergenekon and Sledgehammer, 2015–16

implications: Exposure is usually an accident — a list found while searching for something else — and it rarely comes from the oversight bodies that should have found the network. What follows is often driven by politics as much as evidence: purges can sweep in people who were never members, and reversals can let real members return. The public is left unsure which version to believe. For a reader, the pattern is to ask, of any infiltration story, which stage it is at, who exposed it and why then, and whether a court has yet tested it.
